servicesIndustries.name: Wholesale Trade
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Wholesale trade output rose 1.8% month-over-month against the March 2026 reference period, the second-largest services M/M move in the table — the gain runs ahead of retail at -0.6% M/M and +0.8% Y/Y, a divergence that points to inventory and intermediate-goods turnover outpacing final-sale activity.1 Year-over-year the sector is +1.0%, modest in absolute terms but among the steadier services Y/Y reads alongside Real Estate at +1.8% and Other Services at +0.7%.1

No standalone wholesale tag exists in the project database — capex for the sector is largely leasehold improvement and falls below province GDP thresholds, so activity surfaces indirectly through the 679-project transport & warehousing pipeline ($54.0B priced) where port and distribution-centre builds appear.2 Bill S-214 (Special Economic Measures Act, third reading 2026-05-26 in the Senate) carries direct compliance implications for cross-border wholesale transactions with sanctioned counterparties.3 If S-214 receives Royal Assent, NAICS 41 compliance costs would rise on a subset of cross-border flows, and the M/M strength would need confirmation in the next StatCan release before being treated as durable.

servicesIndustries.name: Retail Trade
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Retail trade GDP slid 0.6% month-over-month for the March reference period while holding +0.8% year-over-year — the M/M decline matches Construction at -0.6% M/M and ranks as the second-weakest services M/M reading behind Accommodation & Food Services at -0.4% M/M and +0.5% Y/Y.1 The divergence between Retail -0.6% M/M and Wholesale Trade +1.8% M/M points to inventory builds at the wholesale stage that are not yet clearing the final-sale channel.1

The project database carries no dedicated retail tag — retail capex generally lands below province GDP thresholds, so the sector is GDP-tracked rather than pipeline-tracked, with the Buffalo Run Real Canadian Superstore (Alberta, Under Construction as of 2026-06-15, Loblaw proponent) currently mis-bucketed under the "Other" fall-through tag pending re-classification.2 If Wholesale Trade +1.8% M/M strength feeds through to retail in the next release, the M/M decline could reverse. If consumer spending weakness persists, the +0.8% Y/Y line would compress further. The procurement.json publishing gap removes federal and provincial consumer-program contract-award visibility that normally corroborates retail capex signals.3

servicesIndustries.name: Finance & Insurance
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Finance & insurance GDP held flat month-over-month at +3.6% year-over-year, the largest services Y/Y reading in the table — the M/M flat print follows a steady accumulation rather than a recent acceleration, with Transportation +3.1% Y/Y and Information +3.2% Y/Y close behind and Real Estate +1.8% Y/Y a tier below.1 The TSX Infrastructure equity basket at 57.56 (+33.0% Y/Y) signals investor risk appetite into capital-intensive sectors, indirectly funding the $614.3B utilities and $54.0B transportation pipelines.2

servicesIndustries.name: Professional, Scientific & Technical Services
servicesIndustries.analysis:

No standalone NAICS-54 project tag exists in the database — engineering and architectural firms instead appear as proponents on infrastructure files (Englobe Corp postings in Ottawa and Regina, for example), with the 1,637 infrastructure-tagged projects ($223.9B priced) representing the indirect pipeline that drives sector demand.2 The job-postings record shows engineering services hiring continuing across CMAs.2 If infrastructure capex velocity picks up — Alto progressing past Under Review, Sydney NS BESS Approved — engineering billings would recover. servicesIndustries.name: Management of Companies & Enterprises
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Management of companies and enterprises GDP fell 22.7% year-over-year, an order of magnitude beyond any other sector reading in the table — the next-largest services Y/Y decline is Education at -2.8% Y/Y, and Manufacturing at -2.5% Y/Y rounds out the comparison set.1 M/M is also down at -1.3%, continuing the direction.1 NAICS 55 is a thin head-office aggregation series that can swing on a single re-classification or large holding-company transaction, and a flag is attached pending StatCan Daily release-note review for Table 36-10-0434.2

No project pipeline tie exists for NAICS 55 — head-office activity does not produce trackable capex at the project level, so the sector is GDP-tracked only and depends on StatCan attribution work for interpretation.3 The move likely reflects either a one-time head-office re-classification or ongoing holding-company restructuring; if the former, the Y/Y line would normalize once the comparison period rolls forward; if the latter, the Y/Y reading would persist negative for multiple quarters. The procurement.json publishing gap removes corroborating federal contract-award context that might otherwise help attribute the size of the move.4

servicesIndustries.name: Public Administration
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Public administration GDP rose 0.4% month-over-month and +1.1% year-over-year, steady-positive across both axes — the reading sits behind Healthcare +2.0% Y/Y and Finance +3.6% Y/Y in the services Y/Y rank but ranks above the flat or negative cohort that includes Education -2.8% Y/Y and Management -22.7% Y/Y.1 Pipeline activity is broad with 27 new files this week across government, defence, and Indigenous tags.2

The combined government, defence, and Indigenous pipeline tracks 278 active projects ($101.7B priced) with defence accounting for $85.9B led by River-class destroyer program (HMCS Fraser entered Under Construction in Nova Scotia) — new this week: CFB Petawawa Military Housing (ON, Proposed), Brockville Correctional Complex and St. Lawrence Valley CTC Expansion (ON, Approved), Shoal Lake 40 First Nation Housing ($51M, MB, Approved), and Endayaan Omaa Treaty One Naawi-Oodena ($90.8M, MB, Under Construction).2 Federal legislative file activity was heavy with 20 federal bills logged in policy.json for the week (S-1 railways through S-214 sanctions sample); Bill S-2 Indian Act amendments (second reading and committee referral 2026-02-27) ties directly to 25 Indigenous-tagged projects.3

Procurement.json was empty across the week-of and eight archived weeks — the procurement_monitor that publishes Open Canada proactive disclosure, CanadaBuys CSVs, SEAO OCDS, and DCC awards is reporting zero federal or provincial construction awards over $5M for two months, an implausible result consistent with a publishing-side failure.4 Without that corroboration the federal contract-award visibility into Public Admin capex is degraded and analyst confidence in week-to-week movement is reduced; if River-class destroyer program continues at pace, defence capex maintains its $85.9B weight independent of procurement.json status.2
